specStatements.text: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. The temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
Changing the temperature of a gas, held at constant volume, changes the pressure exerted by the gas.
• explain how the motion of the molecules in a gas is related to both its temperature and its pressure
• explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.

scopeNotes.statement: • explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for a qualitative explanation only, so this content states the direction of the change and its molecular cause — a higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force, so the pressure rises, and the reverse on cooling. No proportionality between pressure and temperature is stated or implied, no pressure–temperature calculations are set, and the kelvin scale and absolute zero are not introduced here. The only calculations in this section are the ones the specification does require, using pressure × volume = constant at constant temperature.

concepts.definition: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Raising the temperature raises that average, so the molecules move faster on average. Individual molecules still have a range of speeds; temperature describes the average, not any one molecule.

Gas pressure arises from the collisions of the moving gas molecules with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady net force spread over the wall area.

A gas is at constant volume when it is sealed in a rigid container that cannot expand or contract, so the space the gas occupies cannot change. Only the temperature and the pressure are free to change.

concepts.term: Pressure and temperature at constant volume
concepts.definition: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure it exerts. Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so the molecules hit the walls more frequently and with more force, and the pressure rises. Cooling has the opposite effect.

misconceptions.question: A sealed rigid can of gas is warmed. Why does the pressure inside it rise?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they strike the walls more often and each strike exerts a greater force.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules themselves swell up when the gas is heated, and the bigger molecules press harder on the walls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet thermal expansion of solids and liquids first and carry 'heating makes things bigger' down to the particle scale. Diagrams that draw hot gas particles as larger circles reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: Heating changes how fast the molecules move, not how big they are. The size of a molecule does not change with temperature. It is the greater average kinetic energy — faster molecules, more frequent and harder collisions — that raises the pressure.

misconceptions.question: What is the temperature of a gas related to?
misconceptions.correct: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of the gas.
misconceptions.misconception: The total kinetic energy of all the molecules added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a large hot object stores more energy than a small one at the same temperature, and conclude that temperature must measure the total. The word 'average' is easy to drop when reciting the statement.
misconceptions.correction: Two containers of the same gas at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy even if one holds ten times as many molecules and therefore ten times the total energy. Temperature tracks the average, not the total.

misconceptions.question: Do all the molecules in a sample of gas move at the same speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. They move at a wide range of speeds, and each molecule's speed changes at every collision.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes — at a given temperature every molecule moves at the same fixed speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook animations show identical particles bouncing about identically, so 'random' is read as random direction only. The single value implied by 'the temperature' encourages a single value for speed too.
misconceptions.correction: The motion is random in both speed and direction. Collisions constantly redistribute energy, so at any instant some molecules are fast and some are slow. Only the average kinetic energy is fixed by the temperature.

misconceptions.question: Does gas pressure in a sealed container act downwards, like weight?
misconceptions.correct: No. It acts at right angles to every surface the gas touches, including the lid of the container.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas pressure acts downwards, because the weight of the gas presses on the surface below it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is often introduced with a block resting on a table, where the force really is the weight acting downwards. Students transfer that single-direction picture to gases.
misconceptions.correction: Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, and these happen on the base, the sides and the lid of a container alike. The weight of the gas is negligible compared with the force from those collisions.

misconceptions.question: A fixed mass of gas expands into a larger volume at constant temperature. Why does the pressure fall?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so fewer collisions happen each second on each square metre of wall.
misconceptions.misconception: Each molecule hits the wall more gently, because spreading out makes the molecules lose kinetic energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'spread out' with 'weaker' and assume that having more space costs the molecules energy. Constant temperature is stated but is not connected to constant average speed.
misconceptions.correction: At constant temperature the average kinetic energy — and so the force of a typical impact — is unchanged. What changes is the rate of collisions: a bigger space means longer journeys between hits, so the pressure falls.

misconceptions.question: A gas is heated in a rigid sealed container that cannot change volume. What happens to its pressure?
misconceptions.correct: The pressure rises, because the faster molecules hit the walls more often and harder.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure stays the same, because the gas is trapped and cannot expand.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link pressure changes to volume changes only. If nothing can move, they conclude that nothing can change, forgetting that the molecular motion has changed.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure depends on how the molecules move, not only on the space available. Heating raises their average kinetic energy, so collisions with the fixed walls become more frequent and more forceful and the pressure rises.

misconceptions.question: What produces the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
misconceptions.correct: The collisions of the moving molecules with the walls.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules repel one another and push outwards on the walls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have met electrostatic repulsion look for a force acting between particles at a distance, and 'a gas fills its container' sounds like something is pushing the particles apart.
misconceptions.correction: Gas molecules exert almost no force on each other except during the brief moments they collide. Pressure comes from the impacts themselves — countless collisions each second, each giving the wall a tiny push.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the molecules of a gas is correct?

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to their average kinetic energy.
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: the molecules of a gas are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is set by their total kinetic energy.
options.rationale: The first half is right, which makes it tempting; students who know a bigger hot sample stores more energy swap 'average' for 'total'.

options.text: They all move at one single fixed speed, and the temperature of the gas is set by that shared speed.
options.rationale: Animations show identical particles moving identically, so 'random' is read as random direction only, with one speed for all.

options.text: They move along fixed repeating paths, and the temperature of the gas is set by their spacing.
options.rationale: Treats how far apart the molecules are, rather than how fast they move, as what temperature measures — the picture students hold of a hot gas as a spread-out one.

mcqs.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated and the temperature of the gas rises. What happens to the molecules of the gas?

options.text: They all speed up by exactly the same amount and keep sharing one common speed.
options.rationale: Keeps the idea of a single shared speed for every molecule, which survives because diagrams rarely show a spread of speeds.

options.text: Their average kinetic energy rises, so the molecules move faster on average.
options.rationale: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so raising the temperature raises that average and the molecules move faster on average.

options.text: Each molecule expands, so the gas now fills more of the container space.
options.rationale: Carries 'heating makes things bigger' from the thermal expansion of solids down to the particle scale.

options.text: They collide with one another less often, now that they have energy.
options.rationale: Sounds plausible if a student pictures energetic molecules escaping each other, but faster molecules in the same space collide more often, not less.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?

options.text: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
options.rationale: Links pressure changes to volume changes only, so a container that cannot move seems to rule out any change at all.

options.text: It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.
options.rationale: Combines 'heating makes particles bigger' with the idea that spacing sets the pressure; in a rigid container the molecules cannot spread out at all.

options.text: It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
options.rationale: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure exerted: the faster molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force.

options.text: It rises briefly, then falls back to its old value.
options.rationale: Assumes the gas 'settles' after heating, as students expect of a system returning to equilibrium; at the new steady temperature the higher pressure is maintained.

mcqs.stem: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?

options.text: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
options.rationale: Students who have met electrostatic repulsion look for a force acting between particles at a distance to explain why a gas fills its container.

options.text: The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.
options.rationale: Pressure is first taught with a block on a table, where the force really is a weight acting downwards, and that picture is carried over to gases.

options.text: The molecules swelling up and pressing against the walls.
options.rationale: Treats particle size, rather than particle motion, as the source of the push on the wall.

options.text: The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.
options.rationale: Gas pressure comes from the huge number of collisions the randomly moving molecules make with the walls each second, each collision exerting a small force.

mcqs.stem: Two identical rigid sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 20 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. Why is the pressure in flask Y higher?

options.text: The molecules in Y have swollen to a larger size, so they press harder on the walls.
options.rationale: Applies thermal expansion to the molecules themselves rather than to their motion.

options.text: The molecules in Y have a greater average kinetic energy, so they hit the walls harder.
options.rationale: The higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so in the same fixed volume the collisions with the walls are both more frequent and more forceful.

options.text: The molecules in Y repel one another far more strongly at the higher temperature.
options.rationale: Keeps repulsion between molecules as the source of pressure and makes that repulsion depend on temperature.

options.text: The molecules in Y are packed more closely together than those in flask X.
options.rationale: The flasks are identical and sealed, so the same number of molecules occupies the same volume; spacing cannot be the difference.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is cooled while its volume is kept constant. Using the particle model, what happens to the pressure of the gas?

options.text: It stays the same, because the rigid container will not let the gas shrink at all.
options.rationale: Assumes pressure can only change if the volume changes, so a rigid container seems to freeze the pressure.

options.text: It increases, because the cooled molecules move closer to the walls of it.
options.rationale: Borrows contraction on cooling from solids and liquids and treats closeness to the wall, rather than collision rate, as the cause of pressure.

options.text: It decreases, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and less hard.
options.rationale: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules collide with the walls both less frequently and with less force, and the pressure falls.

options.text: It decreases, because the molecules shrink in size as the gas cools down.
options.rationale: Reaches the right direction by the wrong mechanism — particle size does not change with temperature.
